findings.title: A second divine station ends in lost support
findings.claim: The focus treats the forbidden extra deity as a status assigned alongside Allah, then ends in a blamed, seated, unsupported state. Wider echoes make that consequence bodily and social: a would-be companion cannot supply support, the repeated sitting-and-blame formula follows another prohibited act, and 17:39 repeats this prohibition with expulsion as its changed endpoint.
findings.mechanism: The focus verb تجعَل governs إِلَٰهًا آخَرَ and can carry state assignment; 27:61 returns to جعل in a world-ordering scene before asking whether a deity is with Allah, while 21:22 links plural gods with corruption. These independent returns make the added deity a rival station rather than a being created from nothing. At the result, the focus's maʿa relation meets makhdhul, and 18:43 supplies the contrast of a person with no group able to help except God. The focus's taqʿuda also meets 17:29's repeated sitting-and-blame result; 17:39 repeats the same prohibition but changes the endpoint to being cast away. Together these contacts turn the result into loss of bodily agency and backing, with the later reprise setting sitting beside expulsion.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see the added deity as a claimed source of companionship that fails: the person is left without backing or footing, and the later reprise gives that arrested state an expulsion-shaped counterpart.
findings.containment: The ordinary warning against assigning another deity alongside Allah remains intact, as do blame and being left unsupported. The naming branch of jaʿala is unresolved and is kept alongside the state-assignment reading, not ranked against it. Taqʿuda may mark becoming or entry into a state, so bodily sitting, weak legs, inability to rise, and a broken support-link remain analogical resonances; no illness, literal injury, or actual group separation is asserted. 17:29 concerns giving, not idolatry, and 17:39 is a repeated warning rather than a chronological event after 17:22. Connection targets supply Arabic but no target morphology.

epistemic.reason: The focus carriers and exact target Arabic in the connection rows ground the central relation. Several bodily or broken-connection facets are analogical, and the represented reader summaries are legacy-unbound, so the reading is retained with those limits explicit.

findings.title: Another carries a qualified temporal horizon
findings.claim: The focus adjective akhar remains another deity while it can also carry a qualified temporal-horizon resonance: the supplied 16:22 connection pairs one deity with belief in al-akhirah, bringing the rival into a wider question of ultimate orientation.
findings.mechanism: The focus carrier akhar is an adjective for another or not the only one. In 16:22, the supplied exact Arabic names one deity and then mentions al-akhirah; the same root's temporal branch therefore contacts the focus otherness through a wider singular-deity/Hereafter pairing, changing the rival from a second object alone into a possible alternative horizon of orientation.
findings.reader_payoff: The word other can be heard beside a temporal horizon as well as a second object of worship, without losing the focus's ordinary relation of rivalry.
findings.containment: The focus uses a masculine adjective modifying ilah, while 16:22 contains the distinct afterlife noun. Shared root and contextual pairing do not make the focus word literally mean the Hereafter or prove a temporal mechanism. Ordinary polysemy remains a live counter-reading, and the temporal association is exploratory.

epistemic.reason: An exact wider surface and a focus carrier support a same-root association, but the temporal-horizon change is multi-step and form-distant; ordinary polysemy remains equally visible.
